670:
To amend something means to make a specific change to something that already exists — usually to fix, improve, or update it.

The single most important thing to understand about this word is that when you amend something, you are not throwing it away and starting over. You are taking something that is already there, keeping most of it, and making a targeted change to a part of it.

Think of it like editing a letter you've already written. You don't crumple it up and write a new one — you cross out a line, correct a word, or add a sentence. That is the spirit of "amend."

1. Laws and Official Documents

This is where "amend" is used most often. Governments, courts, and organizations regularly amend laws, contracts, rules, and policies when something needs to be corrected or updated.

  • "The parliament voted to amend the law to include stricter penalties."
  • "The company amended its privacy policy after customer complaints."
  • "The lawyer asked the judge for permission to amend the contract."

The change is official, intentional, and documented. The original document still exists — it just has a new version with the changes applied.

2. Spoken or Written Statements

You can amend something you said or wrote if you realize it was incorrect or incomplete. In this case, it simply means going back and correcting yourself — formally or informally.

  • "I'd like to amend what I said earlier. I mentioned the meeting is on Monday, but it's actually on Wednesday."
  • "The spokesperson amended her earlier remarks after new information came to light."

This is a polite, slightly formal way of saying "I need to correct something I said."

3. Behavior (Formal / Old-Fashioned)

Less common in modern everyday speech, "amend" can refer to changing one's behavior or habits — usually to become better.

  • "After the scandal, he promised to amend his ways."

You'll mostly see this in older books or formal writing. In modern conversation, people would more likely say "change his ways" or "turn over a new leaf."

4. Soil (In Gardening)

This is a specific, technical use. To amend soil means to add materials to it to improve its quality — such as adding compost, fertilizer, or sand to make it better for growing plants.

  • "Before planting, she amended the soil with compost."

The logic is the same — you're not replacing the soil entirely; you're improving what's already there.
The Key Nuance: Targeted Change, Not Total Replacement

"Amend" always implies a partial, deliberate change — not a complete overhaul. This is what separates it from words like "replace" or "rewrite" or "abolish."

Imagine a rulebook with 50 rules. If you amend Rule 12, you are changing Rule 12 specifically — the other 49 rules stay exactly as they were. If you replaced the rulebook, you'd throw away all 50 rules and write new ones.

This is why "amend" is the go-to word in legal and official settings — it signals precision. You're touching exactly what needs to be touched, nothing more.

The best real-world example is the United States Constitution. When Americans wanted to add new rights — like freedom of speech, or the right to vote — they didn't rewrite the whole Constitution. They amended it. These additions are literally called Amendments (e.g., "The First Amendment," "The Nineteenth Amendment"). The original document remained; it was simply updated with officially approved changes.

The noun form of "amend" is amendment, which refers to the actual change that was made.

  • "The senators debated the amendment for hours." (They debated the specific change being proposed.)
  • "The contract was signed after a few minor amendments were agreed upon."

So: you amend something → the result of that action is an amendment.

These words are close in meaning but carry different shades:

Amend vs. Change / Alter / Modify
These three are more general and neutral. "Amend" carries a slightly more formal and purposeful tone — it suggests the change is being made to fix or improve something, often in an official context. You'd "amend" a law, but you'd "change" your shirt.

Amend vs. Revise
"Revise" often implies a broader, more thorough reworking — like revising an entire essay. "Amend" is narrower — a specific fix to a specific part.

Amend vs. Correct
"Correct" focuses purely on fixing an error. "Amend" can include fixing errors, but it can also mean updating or improving something that wasn't necessarily wrong to begin with — just outdated or incomplete.

This phrase sounds related to "amend," and in spirit it is — but it has a distinct meaning you should know.

"Make amends" means to apologize or compensate for something wrong you did — to try to repair the harm caused to someone.

  • "After lying to his friend, he wanted to make amends." (He wanted to apologize and make things right.)

Notice the difference:

  • Amend = change/fix a document, law, statement, or situation.
  • Make amends = repair a relationship or make up for a wrongdoing toward someone.

What it meansTo make a specific change to something already existing — to fix, improve, or update it
Key ideaPartial, targeted change. Not a complete replacement.
Most common contextLaws, contracts, official documents
Also used forCorrecting statements, improving behavior, enriching soil
Related nounAmendment
Don't confuse with"Make amends" (to apologize/compensate for wrongdoing)

The next time you see a politician talking about "amending a bill" or a company saying it has "amended its terms," you'll know exactly what they mean: something already written is being carefully changed — improved, corrected, or updated — while the rest stays in place.
671:
When something is described as amended, it means it has been officially or deliberately changed, corrected, or updated — but it has not been thrown away and replaced with something entirely new. The original still exists as the foundation; only certain specific parts of it have been modified.

Think of it this way: imagine you wrote a set of rules for a game. Later, you realize one rule is unfair, so you cross it out and write a better rule in its place. The result is an amended set of rules — it is still recognizably the same document, but improved in a targeted way.

The word carries a few important qualities that make it different from a simple, casual change:

1. The change is intentional and purposeful.
Something is not accidentally amended. There is a clear reason behind the modification — to fix an error, to add missing information, to update outdated content, or to make something fairer, clearer, or more accurate.

2. The original is preserved as a base.
An amended thing is not a completely fresh creation. It is the same thing — the same law, contract, document, or plan — but with specific parts altered. The old version still sits underneath the new one.

3. There is usually a sense of formality or seriousness.
"Amended" is especially common in official, legal, governmental, or professional settings. It signals that the change went through some deliberate process, not just a quick, casual edit.

This is important: an amended version has undergone targeted, specific changes — not a complete overhaul. If someone rewrites an entire document from scratch, that is not "amending" it — that is replacing it. Amending is more surgical. You touch only what needs to be touched and leave the rest as it is.
Where You Will Commonly See It

In law and government:
This is where "amended" is most famous. Laws, constitutions, and bills get amended all the time as societies evolve and new situations arise. A classic example is the U.S. Constitution, which has been amended 27 times. Each amendment changed or added something specific without scrapping the whole document. You might hear: "the amended law," "an amended bill," or "the amended clause."

In contracts and agreements:
When two parties sign a contract but later need to change one of the terms, they don't tear it up — they produce an amended contract that reflects the new agreed-upon terms. The rest of the contract stays exactly the same.

In tax and financial filings:
If you file your tax return and later realize you made a mistake, you can submit an amended tax return — the same form, but corrected.

In proposals and reports:
In professional or academic settings, someone might submit an amended proposal after receiving feedback — one that keeps the original structure but addresses specific concerns that were raised.
How It Compares to Similar Words

These words are close but not identical:

  • Changed — very broad and neutral. Anything that is different from before is "changed." "Amended" is more specific: it implies purpose, formality, and the idea that the original still underlies the new version.
  • Revised — similar to amended, but "revised" can imply a more thorough or comprehensive reworking. You might revise an entire essay. You typically amend a specific clause, section, or point.
  • Corrected — suggests fixing something that was wrong. "Amended" is broader: it includes fixing errors, but also adding new information, updating old content, or making improvements even when nothing was strictly wrong.
  • Replaced — the original is gone and something entirely new takes its place. "Amended" is the opposite of this — the original lives on, just modified.
  • Edited — casual and general, often used for writing. "Amended" carries more weight and formality, and is rarely used for everyday edits.

• "The amended contract now includes a new payment deadline."

(The original contract still exists, but the payment terms have been officially changed.)

  • "Parliament passed the amended version of the bill."

(The bill went through the legislative process, specific parts were changed, and now this updated version has been approved.)

  • "She filed an amended tax return after realizing she had forgotten to include one source of income."

(She submitted the same form again, but with a correction.)

  • "The amended rules now allow players under 18 to participate."

(The original rulebook was modified — specifically the age restriction — without being thrown out entirely.)

  • "After the committee raised concerns, the director submitted an amended proposal."

(The same proposal, updated to address the specific concerns.)
A Simple Test to Know If "Amended" Is the Right Word

Ask yourself three questions:

  1. Does the original still exist as the foundation? ✓
  2. Were only specific parts changed, not the whole thing? ✓
  3. Was the change deliberate and purposeful (not accidental)? ✓

If the answer to all three is yes, "amended" is the right word.

Amended describes something that has been improved or corrected in a deliberate, specific way, while keeping the original largely intact. It is a word that lives in the space between "nothing changed" and "everything is new." It tells you: this thing has evolved — carefully and on purpose — without losing its identity.
672:
An amendment is a formal change, correction, or addition made to something that already exists — most often a document, a law, or an agreement — without completely replacing or throwing away the original.

The single most important thing to understand about an amendment is this: you are not starting over. You are modifying. The original thing stays, but a specific part of it is altered, removed, or added to. Think of it like editing a letter you already wrote — you're not writing a brand new letter, you're fixing or improving the one you have.
Breaking It Down With Everyday Logic

Imagine you and a friend made a written agreement that said: "We will meet every Saturday at 3 PM." Later, both of you decide that 4 PM works better. Instead of tearing up the agreement and writing a whole new one, you both agree to officially change just that one part. That official change? That is an amendment to your agreement.

The word can refer to:

  • The act of changing something ("the amendment of the law took months")
  • The specific change itself ("read Amendment No. 3 carefully")
Where You'll Most Commonly Encounter This Word

1. Laws and Legislation

When a government passes a law, it doesn't always get everything perfect the first time. Later, lawmakers may need to update it. Rather than scrapping the entire law, they pass an amendment — a carefully worded official change that plugs into the existing law and alters only what needs altering.

For example: A road safety law might originally set a speed limit of 60 mph. Years later, an amendment might change it to 55 mph on certain roads. Everything else in the law remains untouched.

2. Constitutions

This is where the word is most famous. A constitution is the supreme law of a country, and it is written to last a very long time. But societies change, and sometimes the constitution must change with them. Those changes are called amendments.

The most well-known real-world example is the United States Constitution. The original document was written in 1787. Since then, it has been amended 27 times. The first ten amendments, added in 1791, are so important and famous that they have their own collective name: the Bill of Rights. Each amendment addresses something specific:

  • The 1st Amendment protects freedom of speech, religion, and the press.
  • The 2nd Amendment addresses the right to bear arms.
  • The 13th Amendment (added in 1865) abolished slavery.
  • The 19th Amendment (added in 1920) gave women the right to vote.

Notice that in each case, the original Constitution was not thrown out — it was built upon. Each amendment became a permanent, numbered addition to the document.

3. Contracts and Agreements

In business and law, contracts are formal written agreements between two or more parties. Once signed, a contract is legally binding. But situations change — prices, timelines, conditions. When both parties agree to officially change something in the contract, that change is documented in an amendment to the contract.

For example, a construction contract originally might say a building must be completed by June 1st. If delays occur and both sides agree to a new deadline of August 1st, they sign an amendment that updates just that detail. The rest of the contract stays exactly as it was.

4. Proposals, Reports, and Motions (in Meetings)

In formal meetings — whether a corporate boardroom, a city council, or a school committee — when someone puts forward a proposal (called a motion), others can suggest changes to it before it gets voted on. Those suggested changes are called amendments to the motion. For example, someone proposes spending $10,000 on new equipment. Another member suggests an amendment: change the amount to $8,000. The group then votes on whether to accept that amendment before voting on the full proposal.

5. Tax Returns

In many countries, if you file your taxes and later realize you made a mistake, you are allowed to file an amended return — an officially corrected version of your original tax filing. The document you submit to correct it is called an amendment (or an amended return). You are not filing your taxes from scratch; you are formally patching the original filing.
The Defining Qualities of an Amendment

Understanding what makes something an amendment (rather than just a casual change) comes down to three qualities:

It is formal. An amendment is not a scribbled note in the margin or a verbal agreement. It is an official, recognized, and recorded change that goes through a proper process — a vote, a signature, an official filing, etc.

It is specific. An amendment targets particular parts of a document. It doesn't rewrite everything. It says, in effect: "In this document, change this specific thing to this." The rest of the original is untouched.

It becomes part of the original. Once an amendment is accepted, it is not a separate side-document that people might forget about. It is incorporated into the understanding of the original document. When people refer to the US Constitution today, the 27 amendments are fully part of what "the Constitution" means.

An amendment is almost always used in a neutral or positive sense. It implies a considered, deliberate improvement or correction — not a random or hasty scribble. When someone says a law was amended, it carries the implication that there was a reason, a process, and an official sanction behind that change. This is what distinguishes an amendment from simply "a change" or "an edit."

An amendment is an officially approved and formally recorded change — whether a correction, an addition, or a modification — made to an existing document, law, agreement, or proposal, without discarding the original entirely.

It is the word the world uses when something important and established needs to be updated carefully, deliberately, and on the record.
673: An amenity is anything — a feature, a service, a facility, or even an agreeable quality — that makes a place, situation, or experience more comfortable, convenient, or enjoyable. Think of it as the "nice extras" that go beyond what is merely necessary. A house needs walls and a roof. A rooftop garden, a gym, or a swimming pool? Those are amenities.

1. Physical Features and Facilities (Most Common Use)

This is by far the most common way the word is used today. An amenity here is a concrete, tangible feature — something you can see, use, or access — that adds comfort or convenience to a place.

Examples across different settings:

  • Hotel: A luxury hotel might offer amenities such as a spa, a rooftop pool, free Wi-Fi, a concierge service, and complimentary breakfast.
  • Apartment building: Residents enjoy amenities like a gym, a parking garage, a package locker room, and a communal lounge.
  • Neighbourhood or city: People are drawn to areas with great amenities — good schools, parks, restaurants, public transport, libraries, and shops all count.
  • Office: A modern workplace might offer amenities like a coffee bar, nap pods, or a terrace — things that attract and keep employees.

The key idea is that these features are desirable additions, not bare essentials. They improve the experience of being somewhere.

2. A Pleasant or Agreeable Quality (More Formal/Literary Use)

In this older, slightly more formal sense, "amenity" (often used in the singular) refers to the general pleasantness or agreeableness of something — not a specific feature, but a quality.

  • "The amenity of the climate drew many retirees to the coastal town."
    → The pleasant, mild, comfortable nature of the weather.
  • "She loved the amenity of village life — the quiet, the clean air, the slow pace."
    → The overall agreeable, comfortable character of that lifestyle.

You're less likely to encounter this sense in everyday conversation, but you will find it in books, formal writing, and some travel or real estate descriptions.

3. Social Amenities — Polite Behaviours in Social Situations

This is a specific and interesting use of the word. Social amenities are the small acts of courtesy, polite gestures, and pleasantries that people exchange to make social situations smooth and comfortable.

  • "Before getting into the serious business negotiations, the two sides exchanged social amenities — handshakes, compliments about the weather, and brief small talk."
  • "She was exhausted and had no patience left for social amenities; she went straight to the point."

Think of social amenities as the social "lubricant" — the "Hello, how are you?", the polite smile, the small compliment, the handshake. None of these are strictly necessary to get something done, but they make human interaction more pleasant and respectful. They follow the same logic as the word's other meanings: extras that add comfort and ease.

You will often hear the phrase "basic amenities", and it's worth paying attention to. In this phrase, the word shifts slightly to refer to the fundamental comforts of modern living — running water, electricity, sanitation, heating. While these are technically necessities, the phrase "basic amenities" is widely used, especially when describing places that lack even these minimum standards of comfort.

  • "The remote village still lacked basic amenities like clean water and electricity."

So "amenity" can stretch from meaning a luxury extra (a rooftop pool) all the way down to a fundamental comfort (clean water), depending on context.

• Amenity (singular) — used when talking about one specific feature, or the general quality of pleasantness ("the amenity of the garden").
  • Amenities (plural) — far more common in everyday use. When people list the features of a hotel, flat, or neighbourhood, they almost always say "amenities."
    • "What amenities does the apartment have?"
    • "The gym and pool are among the best amenities in this building."
The Underlying Logic of the Word

No matter which sense you encounter, one thread runs through all of them: amenity always points to something that adds comfort, pleasantness, or ease — something that improves an experience beyond the bare minimum. Whether it's a hotel spa, a park down the road, pleasant weather, or a polite handshake — an amenity makes things nicer than they would otherwise be.

Ask yourself: "Does this feature/quality make the place or situation more comfortable, convenient, or enjoyable — even though it isn't strictly necessary to function?"

If yes → it's an amenity.
674:
An amethyst is a beautiful purple gemstone. More specifically, it is a type of quartz — one of the most common minerals on Earth — but what makes amethyst special is its striking purple or violet color. Quartz by itself is usually clear or white, but when tiny amounts of iron get trapped inside it during its formation deep in the Earth, and natural radiation acts on that iron over millions of years, the quartz turns purple. That purple quartz is what we call amethyst.

It belongs to the category of semi-precious gemstones, meaning it is genuinely precious and beautiful but is generally considered a step below the "big four" (diamonds, rubies, emeralds, and sapphires) in terms of rarity and price. That said, fine-quality amethysts with a deep, rich purple can still be quite valuable.

The defining feature of amethyst is its purple color. But "purple" is a wide range — and amethyst covers much of it. The color can go from:

  • A very pale, almost pinkish-lilac (like soft lavender)
  • To a medium violet
  • To a deep, rich, royal purple

The most prized amethysts are a deep, saturated purple, sometimes with a slight reddish or bluish tint. Gems that are too pale or too dark (almost black-purple) are considered less desirable.

Amethyst crystals are usually transparent to translucent, meaning light can pass through them. When well-cut and polished, they have a beautiful glassy shine.
How It Forms and Where It Is Found

Amethyst grows inside geodes — hollow rocks or cavities inside the earth that are lined on the inside with crystals. Imagine cracking open a dull, grey rock and finding a stunning cluster of sparkling purple crystals inside. That is a geode. Amethyst crystals grow slowly over millions of years as mineral-rich water fills these cavities and the minerals crystallize.

Amethyst is found in many parts of the world, but the major sources are:

  • Brazil — The world's largest producer. Brazilian amethyst tends to be lighter in color and comes in enormous quantities.
  • Uruguay — Produces smaller amounts, but the color is often much darker and more intense. Uruguayan amethysts are highly prized.
  • Zambia (Africa) — Known for producing deep-colored, high-quality stones.
  • Russia (Siberia) — Historically famous for "Siberian amethyst," which has a deep purple with flashes of red and blue and is considered among the finest in the world.
  • Other sources include India, South Korea, Austria, and parts of the United States.

Amethyst is harder than most everyday materials but softer than a diamond. On the Mohs scale (a 1–10 scale that measures how scratch-resistant a mineral is), amethyst scores a 7. This means:

  • It is hard enough to resist scratches from most things in daily life (like keys or glass).
  • But it can still be scratched by harder stones like topaz (8), sapphire (9), or diamond (10).
  • Its hardness makes it well-suited for everyday jewelry like rings, bracelets, and necklaces.

Its crystal structure is hexagonal (six-sided) — if you look at a raw, unpolished amethyst crystal, you will often see it has a pointed, six-sided shape like a pillar.

Not all amethysts are the same. There are a few notable varieties and related stones worth knowing:

  • Siberian amethyst: The name given to top-quality deep purple amethysts (regardless of where they actually come from today). Rich purple with red and blue flashes.
  • Rose de France: A pale, almost pinkish-purple variety of amethyst. Lighter and more delicate-looking.
  • Ametrine: A fascinating natural gemstone that is half amethyst (purple) and half citrine (yellow quartz) in the same crystal. It forms naturally in Bolivia when temperature differences occur during the crystal's growth. The result is a stone with two colors — purple on one side, golden-yellow on the other.
  • Prasiolite (also called "green amethyst"): When amethyst is heated to around 470°C (about 880°F), it can turn a pale green. This green version is called prasiolite.
  • Citrine from amethyst: Similarly, heating amethyst often turns it yellow or orange, producing what the market sells as citrine. A large portion of the "citrine" sold in jewelry is actually heat-treated amethyst.
  • Synthetic amethyst: Amethyst can also be grown in laboratories. Lab-created amethysts are chemically identical to natural ones but are much cheaper and have no natural origin.

In Jewelry:
Amethyst is one of the most widely used gemstones in jewelry. It is cut and polished into many shapes — oval, round, pear-shaped, cushion-cut, and more — and set into rings, earrings, necklaces, pendants, bracelets, and brooches. It is often paired with silver or white gold because the cool tones complement the purple, though yellow gold settings also create a rich, vintage look.

As Decorative Objects:
Large amethyst geodes and crystal clusters are kept as decorative pieces in homes and offices. Their natural beauty makes them popular display items.

In Spiritual and Wellness Practices:
Many people use amethyst in crystal healing and meditation. It is widely believed (in spiritual traditions, not science) to promote calmness, clarity, and peace of mind, and to help with sleep and stress. While there is no scientific evidence for these claims, amethyst is one of the most popular crystals in wellness culture.

Amethyst has been treasured by humans for thousands of years, and it carries a rich history.

Ancient Beliefs:
The ancient Greeks and Romans had a fascinating belief about amethyst: they thought wearing it or drinking from cups made of it would prevent drunkenness. People would drink wine from amethyst goblets or wear amethyst jewelry at parties, believing it kept them sober. This belief was widespread enough that amethyst was carved into drinking vessels specifically for this purpose.

Royalty and the Clergy:
For centuries, deep purple was the color of royalty, power, and wealth — because purple dye was extremely rare and expensive in ancient times. Amethyst, being naturally purple, was cherished by kings, queens, and emperors. It was set into crowns, scepters, and royal jewelry across many civilizations. The British Crown Jewels contain notable amethysts. Similarly, Christian bishops and cardinals wore amethyst rings as a symbol of their rank — amethyst was called the "bishop's stone."

Soldiers:
In medieval Europe, soldiers wore amethyst believing it protected them in battle and kept them calm and clear-headed.

Fall From Extreme Rarity:
For a long time, amethyst was as valuable as ruby and sapphire and was among the most prized gemstones in the world. That changed dramatically in the 19th century when enormous deposits were discovered in Brazil. The sudden abundance of supply made amethyst far more affordable and accessible, which is why today it is classified as semi-precious rather than precious. Its beauty, however, remains undisputed.

The word "amethyst" is also used as a color name. When someone says something is "amethyst," they mean it is a medium to deep purple, often with a slightly blue or reddish tone — the color of the gemstone itself. You will encounter this color name in fashion, interior design, art, and cosmetics (lipstick shades, fabric colors, paint names, etc.).

Amethyst is the official birthstone for February, meaning it is the gemstone traditionally associated with people born in that month. It is also linked to the 6th wedding anniversary in some traditions, where couples exchange gifts of amethyst.

AspectDetail

In short: amethyst is a purple variety of quartz that gets its color from iron and natural radiation. It ranges from pale lilac to deep violet, grows inside geodes, and is mined mainly in Brazil, Uruguay, Zambia, and Russia. It is hard enough for everyday jewelry, deeply embedded in the history of royalty and religion, and remains one of the most beloved and widely used gemstones in the world. The word also doubles as the name of the purple color it represents. And if you were an ancient Greek, you would also have believed it kept you sober — which perhaps says something about how much people throughout history have loved this remarkable stone.
675:
Amiability is the quality of being friendly, warm, and pleasant — the kind of natural, easy-going goodness that makes a person genuinely nice to be around. When someone is amiable, amiability is the name we give to that quality they possess.

Think of it this way: if a person is strong, their strength is what you're naming. If a person is amiable, their amiability is what you're naming. It is the noun form of the adjective "amiable," and it refers to a personality trait — a habitual way of being.
What It Actually Means to Have Amiability

A person with amiability tends to:

  • Make people feel comfortable and welcome in their presence
  • Respond to others with warmth rather than coldness or irritability
  • Have a generally cheerful, easy-going manner
  • Be agreeable and cooperative without being difficult or harsh
  • Create a pleasant atmosphere simply by being themselves

Amiability lives in the feeling someone gives you. When you leave a conversation thinking, "That person was so easy to talk to — so warm and pleasant," you've just experienced someone's amiability firsthand.
A Key Distinction: What Amiability Is NOT

This is where learners often get confused, so let's be precise.

Amiability is not the same as mere politeness. Politeness can be cold and mechanical — you can be polite to someone you dislike while keeping them at arm's length. Amiability, by contrast, is genuine. It carries real warmth. An amiable person isn't just following social rules; they are naturally pleasant and likeable.

Amiability is not the same as kindness. Kindness is about doing — performing acts of goodness for others. Amiability is about being — the pleasant, agreeable quality of a person's manner and temperament. A person can be kind but serious and stern in personality (not amiable), or they can be amiable but not particularly selfless (not especially kind). Ideally, of course, a person can be both.

Amiability is not the same as charisma. Charisma is a magnetic, compelling quality that draws people in with force and energy. Amiability is gentler — it's the quiet pleasantness that makes people feel at ease, not necessarily dazzled.

Amiability is not weakness. An amiable person can have firm beliefs and strong character. Their warmth doesn't mean they are pushovers. Amiability describes how someone behaves in their manner and tone, not how resolved they are in their convictions.

Amiability describes a disposition — which means it's not just a mood on a good day, but a steady, habitual way of being. A person who is occasionally pleasant doesn't necessarily have amiability. Amiability implies a consistent quality of warmth and friendliness that others can rely on and feel.

It also carries a subtle note of ease. An amiable person doesn't make social interactions feel forced, tense, or awkward. Their amiability is the quality that smooths things over, puts others at rest, and makes time spent with them feel comfortable and enjoyable.

Amiability is used to describe people, and sometimes the atmosphere or tone that a person creates around them. Here are some natural example sentences:

  • "Her amiability made her instantly popular — strangers felt like old friends within minutes of meeting her."
  • "Despite the tense negotiations, his natural amiability helped keep the discussions calm and civil."
  • "There was a quiet amiability about the old professor that made even nervous students feel confident asking questions."
  • "The guests were charmed by the host's amiability — every person in the room felt genuinely welcomed."

Notice that in each case, amiability is doing something — it's creating an effect, producing a feeling in others. That's the power of the word. It's not just an abstract label; it describes a quality that has a real, tangible impact on the people around someone.

If you had to summarize amiability in one sentence: it is the quality of being genuinely warm, pleasant, and easy to get along with — a consistent, natural friendliness that makes others feel comfortable and welcome.

It is a beautiful word for a beautiful quality, and when you use it, you are saying something more precise and richer than simply calling someone "nice." You are pointing to something deeper — a settled, genuine warmth in a person's character that they carry with them wherever they go.
676:
Amiable describes a person who is genuinely friendly, warm, and pleasant to be around — someone who has a naturally good-natured personality that makes others feel comfortable and at ease.

If someone is amiable, they are the kind of person who is easy to like, easy to talk to, and easy to get along with. There is a quiet, calm warmth to them. They don't cause unnecessary trouble, they don't snap or snarl, and being around them just feels... pleasant.

Think of a neighbor who always greets you with a genuine smile, listens patiently, and never makes you feel unwelcome. That neighbor is amiable.
The Feel of the Word — The Nuance

This is where it gets interesting, because "amiable" is not just a fancy word for "friendly." It carries a specific flavor.

Amiable friendliness is calm and natural, not loud or performative. An amiable person doesn't have to work hard to be liked — their warmth just flows out of them naturally. They are not necessarily the loudest person in the room, the most exciting, or the funniest. They might even be quiet. But there is a genuine, easy warmth about them that draws people in.

Amiable also implies good nature — a kind of inner pleasantness. An amiable person doesn't hold grudges, doesn't get irritated easily, and tends to see the best in others. Their temperament is gentle. They are agreeable without being a pushover, and pleasant without being fake.

So if "friendly" is the general category, "amiable" is a specific type of friendliness — one that is warm, calm, genuine, and good-natured.

Getting the edges of a word right is just as important as getting the center right.

Amiable does not mean exciting or charismatic. A party animal who gets everyone hyped up might be fun and energetic, but that's not what "amiable" describes. Amiable is quieter than that.

Amiable does not mean someone is your close friend. You can describe an acquaintance, a coworker, or even a stranger as amiable. It describes the quality of their personality, not the depth of your bond with them.

Amiable does not mean someone is a pushover or blindly agreeable. An amiable person can disagree with you, hold firm opinions, or say no — but they do so in a pleasant, non-hostile way. Their good nature doesn't disappear when there's conflict; it just means the conflict stays civil.

Amiable does not mean fake cheerfulness. It implies genuine warmth, not a hollow customer-service smile.

Here are examples showing how the word is used naturally:

  • "My new manager is incredibly amiable — she always has time to listen and never makes you feel judged."
  • "Despite their differences, the two politicians managed to have an amiable discussion."
  • "He was a quiet man, but his amiable nature meant everyone at work liked him."
  • "The hotel staff were amiable and helpful throughout our stay."
  • "She greeted every guest with an amiable smile that put them instantly at ease."

Notice that in all of these, the warmth is real, calm, and pleasant — never over-the-top.
How Amiable Compares to Similar Words

Several words are close cousins to "amiable," but each has its own shade of meaning.

Friendly is the broadest and most everyday word. Anyone who is being nice can be called friendly. Amiable is more specific — it describes a deeper, more consistent quality of character, not just a single nice action.

Affable is the closest synonym to amiable. Both describe someone easy to talk to and pleasant in manner. If there's a hair of difference, affable leans slightly more toward someone who is easy to approach and converse with, while amiable leans slightly more toward their overall warmth of personality. In practice, they are often interchangeable.

Genial means warm, cheerful, and sociable — but it carries a slightly more outgoing, hearty energy. A genial person might be a backslapping, jovial type. An amiable person can be quieter and more reserved.

Pleasant is a lighter, more surface-level word. A pleasant person is nice to be around, but it doesn't tell you much about their inner character. Amiable says more — it tells you something about who they genuinely are.

Good-natured is very close to amiable and focuses on the absence of bad temper or malice. An amiable person is definitely good-natured, but amiable also adds the layer of active warmth and friendliness.

Likable describes the effect a person has on others (people like them), while amiable describes the cause — the qualities in that person that make others like them.
When Would You Use This Word?

Because "amiable" is a slightly more formal and literary word, you'd typically see it in writing, professional contexts, or thoughtful speech — rather than in casual everyday chatter (where you'd more likely just say "friendly" or "nice").

You'd use it when you want to describe someone's personality with a bit more depth and precision than "nice" allows. It's a word that signals you've thought about the person carefully, and what you've concluded is that their warmth is genuine, calm, and consistent.

If you had to boil it down to its essence:

Amiable means genuinely warm, calm, and pleasant in personality — the kind of person who is naturally easy to like and get along with.
677:
Amiably means in a friendly, pleasant, and good-natured way. When someone does something amiably, they do it with easy, relaxed warmth — not forced, not stiff, just naturally cheerful and agreeable.

It describes how someone does something. It almost always modifies a verb.

She smiled amiably.
He nodded amiably.
They chatted amiably for an hour.

"Amiably" carries a specific texture that's worth understanding precisely.

Think of someone who is easy to be around — they don't make things awkward, they don't snap at you, they don't put on a fake performance either. They're simply pleasant. Relaxed. Agreeable. That ease and warmth is exactly what "amiably" captures.

It sits between two extremes:

  • It's warmer than "politely" — politeness can be cold and mechanical. Amiably is genuinely friendly.
  • It's lighter than "warmly" or "affectionately" — those words suggest a deeper personal bond. Amiably is more casual, the way you'd be with a friendly acquaintance or a stranger you're getting along with well.

1. In conversation

"I don't agree with you, but I understand your point," he said amiably.

He's disagreeing, but there's no edge to it, no hostility. He says it with an easy, good-natured tone. That's amiably.

2. In behavior

The old man amiably waved at the children running through his garden.

He's not annoyed. He's not forcing a smile. He just waves, pleasantly, naturally.

3. In a social setting

The two strangers talked amiably while waiting for the bus.

They chatted easily, with no tension, no awkwardness — just pleasant, friendly conversation between people who don't know each other well.

• It does not mean deeply loving or emotionally intense. You wouldn't say someone cried amiably or hugged amiably.
  • It does not mean formally polite. A judge who pronounces a verdict very correctly is polite, not amiable.
  • It does not mean excitedly friendly. "Enthusiastically" would carry that energy. Amiably is calmer, more laid-back.
Words Close in Meaning (and How They Differ)

• Pleasantly — similar, but more surface-level. Pleasantly focuses on the effect (it was a pleasant experience). Amiably focuses on the person's natural, easy friendliness.
  • Cheerfully — focuses on good mood and happiness. Amiably focuses more on easygoing friendliness.
  • Cordially — more formal and deliberate, like at an official gathering. Amiably is relaxed and informal.
  • Affably — the closest synonym; almost interchangeable with amiably. Both mean in a friendly, easy-to-approach way.

If you can replace a word with "in a friendly, easygoing, good-natured way" and the sentence still makes perfect sense, amiably fits.

She amiably agreed to help. → She agreed to help in a friendly, easygoing, good-natured way. ✅

Amiably = in a way that is friendly, relaxed, and pleasant — naturally so, without effort or pretense. The person doing it creates no friction, no awkwardness. They are simply easy, warm, and agreeable to be around in that moment.

It's one of those words that, once you know it, you'll start noticing it constantly — in novels, news articles, and conversations — because writers love it for capturing that specific quality of effortless, genuine warmth.
678:
Amicable describes a quality of friendliness, goodwill, and cooperation — specifically in a situation where there could be tension, conflict, or disagreement, but the people involved choose to handle it calmly and respectfully instead.

Think of it this way: when two people have a reason to fight, argue, or be hostile — but they don't. They remain civil, cooperative, and decent toward each other. That quality, that spirit of peaceful goodwill, is what amicable captures.

This word almost always appears in situations involving potential conflict. That's the key. You don't usually call an ordinary friendly lunch "amicable." But a divorce where both partners remain respectful? A business dispute resolved without bitterness? A disagreement settled through calm discussion? Those are the natural homes of this word.

If there's no conflict in sight, people just say friendly. Amicable carries an extra layer of meaning: "this could have gone badly, but it didn't."

Amicable does not mean warm, loving, or enthusiastic. It doesn't mean the people like each other deeply. Two people can have an amicable divorce and still not want to spend time together. What it means is: no hostility, no bitterness, no bad blood. It is friendliness in its most restrained, practical, cooperative form.
Where you'll typically see it (common pairings)

Amicable almost always pairs with words related to agreements, disputes, or endings:

  • an amicable settlement (a legal or financial dispute resolved peacefully)
  • an amicable divorce / separation (ending a marriage without bitterness)
  • an amicable agreement (a deal reached cooperatively)
  • an amicable resolution (a conflict brought to a peaceful close)
  • amicable terms ("they parted on amicable terms" — they ended things without hard feelings)
  • an amicable relationship (a working relationship that is respectful and cooperative, even if not warm)

You'll notice a pattern: these all involve situations where disagreement or friction is natural, but the parties choose decency over hostility.
How it compares to similar words

Civil is the closest cousin. To be civil means to be polite and decent. Amicable goes one step further — it implies genuine goodwill and a cooperative spirit, not just surface-level politeness.

Cordial means warmly polite. It's slightly warmer than amicable and can apply to any social situation, not just tense ones.

Friendly is broader and warmer. Amicable is friendly specifically in the context of potential conflict.

Harmonious focuses on things going smoothly together as a whole. Amicable focuses on the attitude people bring to a situation.

The clearest antonym of amicable is acrimonious — which means bitter, harsh, and full of ill will. These two words are practically mirror images of each other, used in the exact same contexts:

  • an amicable divorce vs. an acrimonious divorce
  • an amicable settlement vs. an acrimonious dispute

Other antonyms include: hostile, antagonistic, bitter, and contentious.
A note on register (how formal it is)

Amicable is a slightly formal word. You'll hear it most in legal, journalistic, and professional settings. Someone might say "they reached an amicable settlement out of court" in a news article, or "the two sides parted on amicable terms" in a business report. In casual everyday speech, people tend to say "friendly" instead — but amicable is perfectly natural in writing and formal conversation.

1. After long negotiations, the two companies reached an amicable agreement without ever going to court.
  2. The couple decided to divorce, but kept things amicable for the sake of their children.
  3. Even though the colleagues disagreed on many things, they maintained an amicable working relationship.
  4. The meeting was tense at first, but both sides made an effort to keep the discussion amicable.
  5. They didn't end up as friends, but they parted on amicable terms — no anger, no resentment.
Amicable means peacefully friendly and cooperative — especially in a situation that could have turned bitter or hostile, but didn't.
679:
Amicably means doing something in a friendly, peaceful, and cooperative way — especially when there is a disagreement, a separation, or a conflict involved, yet people choose to handle it without hostility or bitterness.

Think of it this way: when two people could argue, fight, or become enemies — but instead they stay calm, respectful, and goodwill-filled — they are behaving amicably.

The word carries a very specific emotional weight. It doesn't just mean "friendly" in the way you'd describe chatting with a neighbour. It specifically suggests:

  • There was a potential for conflict, tension, or hurt feelings.
  • Despite that, everyone involved chose to be civil, cooperative, and understanding.
  • The outcome was reached without resentment, hostility, or bitterness.

This is why you'll almost never hear someone say "We had tea amicably." That's too ordinary a situation. The word shines brightest when there's a backdrop of difficulty or disagreement.

1. Ending relationships (romantic or business)

"After ten years of marriage, they divorced amicably and remained close friends."
"The two business partners parted amicably and wished each other well."

2. Resolving disputes or conflicts

"The two countries resolved their border disagreement amicably through dialogue."
"The neighbours settled their property dispute amicably without involving lawyers."

3. Legal or professional settlements

"The lawsuit was settled amicably out of court."
"The employees and management reached an amicable agreement — meaning: they sorted it out in a friendly, cooperative way.

4. Disagreements that end respectfully

"The two candidates debated fiercely but parted amicably after the event."
The Feeling It Creates in a Reader or Listener

When someone says something was done amicably, it signals relief and maturity. It tells you: "Yes, this could have been messy — but it wasn't. Everyone behaved well." It creates a sense of goodwill, dignity, and mutual respect.

• It doesn't just mean "politely." You can be polite but cold and distant. Amicably implies genuine goodwill and warmth, not just surface-level courtesy.
  • It doesn't mean "easily." Something can be hard to resolve but still resolved amicably.
  • It doesn't mean "silently." People may have had long discussions, yet still done it amicably.
